title: Make.com Advanced: Routers, Iterators, Aggregators, and Data Stores
summary: This is where Make.com's visual model really shines, letting you build logic that would be painful in a linear tool. A Router splits your scenario into multiple branches, and each route can have its own filter so different data follows different path
content:
# Make.com Advanced: Routers, Iterators, Aggregators, and Data Stores ##### The order with three items and one very wrong email A student built a Make scenario for a small store: an order webhook arrives, and the customer gets a confirmation email listing what they bought. It worked in testing. Then a customer ordered three products and received an email that said, cheerfully, "Thanks for buying: Mechanical Keyboard." The other two items were in the payload. They were just never seen, because the scenario mapped `items[0].name` — the first element of an array — and nothing told it there were two more. That bug is the doorway to today's material. Real data is not one flat record. It arrives as **arrays inside records**, needs to be **split** so each element can be handled, often needs to be **recombined** into a summary, frequently needs to be **routed** down different paths, and sometimes needs the scenario to **remember** what it already processed. Make gives you four purpose-built tools for exactly these situations, and they are the reason experienced automators reach for Make when things get real. ##### Routers: one input, many branches A **Router** is a module that takes the incoming bundle and sends a copy down *every* route attached to it. Add it from the flow-control menu, drag out as many routes as you need, and each route becomes an independent chain of modules. By itself a router just fans out. The intelligence comes from putting a **filter on each route**: click the wrench icon on the line leaving the router and set a condition. Only routes whose filter passes will execute. Two behaviours to understand precisely: **Routes are evaluated independently, not as if/else-if.** A bundle matching two route filters travels both. If you need mutual exclusivity, write conditions that cannot overlap, or use the **fallback route** — a special route (set via the filter dialog's "Fallback route" checkbox) that runs *only* when no other route matched. That fallback is the difference between graceful handling and silent data loss. **Routes execute in order, left to right, one at a time to completion.** Route 1's entire chain runs before route 2 starts. This matters if route 2 depends on something route 1 created. ```mermaid flowchart LR W((Webhook
new order)) --> R{Router} R -->|total >= 10000| A1((Create CRM deal)) A1 --> A2((Slack #sales)) R -->|total < 10000| B1((Send thank-you email)) R -->|fallback| C1((Log to error sheet)) ``` ##### Filters between modules Filters in Make are not modules — they live **on the connection line** between two modules, which is a smarter design than it first appears. Click the wrench on any route, set a label and a condition, and bundles that fail the condition simply stop there. Because filters sit on lines rather than occupying a module slot, **they cost zero operations**. That makes "filter as early as possible" not just good practice but free good practice. A filter placed immediately after a trigger that emits 200 bundles, keeping only 8, saves you the cost of running every downstream module 192 unnecessary times. Make's condition editor offers text, numeric, date, boolean and array operators, plus the crucial *Exists / Does not exist* pair for optional fields. You can add AND rules within a group and OR across groups. ##### Iterators: splitting an array into bundles Back to the three-item order. Here is the fix. An **Iterator** takes a single bundle containing an array and outputs **one bundle per array element**. That is its entire job, and it is transformative: everything downstream now runs once per item. Add Flow Control → **Iterator**, and in its single field map the array — `{{1.items}}`. If the incoming bundle looks like this: ```json { "order_id": "ORD-1042", "customer": { "name": "Ananya Rao", "email": "ananya@example.com" }, "items": [ { "sku": "KB-01", "name": "Mechanical Keyboard", "qty": 2, "price": 2499.00 }, { "sku": "MS-07", "name": "Wireless Mouse", "qty": 1, "price": 899.00 }, { "sku": "PD-03", "name": "Desk Pad", "qty": 1, "price": 699.00 } ] } ``` ...the Iterator emits three bundles. A Google Sheets "Add a Row" module after it creates three rows. Each bundle exposes the element's fields directly (`{{2.name}}`, `{{2.qty}}`) plus a handy `Bundle order position` value for numbering. Note the cost implication: three bundles × three downstream modules = nine operations. Iterators multiply your operation count, which is why filtering *before* the iterator matters. ##### Aggregators: putting the pieces back together Splitting is half the story. Often you need to reassemble — one summary email, not three; one invoice PDF, not three. An **Aggregator** does the reverse of an Iterator: it consumes many bundles and outputs **one**. The key setting is the **Source Module** dropdown, where you choose which earlier module started the split (usually your Iterator). Everything between that module and the aggregator is treated as the loop body. Make offers several flavours: - **Text Aggregator** — joins values into one string with a separator you choose. Perfect for an email body: `{{name}} x{{qty}} — ₹{{price}}` joined by a newline. - **Array Aggregator** — produces a real array of objects, useful for feeding an API that wants line items as JSON. - **Numeric Aggregator** — sum, average, count, min, max. This is how you compute an order total from the items. - **Table Aggregator** — builds a formatted table, ideal for reports. So the complete pattern for our order becomes: ```text Webhook → Iterator({{1.items}}) → Sheets: Add Row (runs 3x) → Text Aggregator (runs 1x, source = Iterator) → Email: Send (runs 1x, body = aggregated text) ``` The **Iterator/Aggregator relationship** the assignment asks about is exactly this: they are a matched pair defining a loop. The Iterator opens it and fans one bundle into many; the Aggregator closes it and folds many back into one. Modules between them run per item; modules after the Aggregator run once. A common mistake: pointing the aggregator's Source Module at the wrong module, which either aggregates too much (starting from the trigger) or produces one bundle per item anyway. ##### Data stores: giving your scenario a memory Everything so far is **stateless** — each run knows nothing about previous runs. That is fine until you need one of these: - "Skip records I already processed" (deduplication). - "Only alert me if this is a *new* price, not the same one again." - "Keep a running counter across runs." - "Store the timestamp of the last successful sync." A **Data store** is Make's built-in mini-database: a named table with a defined structure (fields with types) and a unique **key** per record. You create it under the Data Stores section, then use the *Data store* modules inside a scenario: - **Get a record** — fetch by key. Returns empty if absent. - **Add/replace a record** — write by key. - **Update a record**, **Delete a record**, **Search records**, **Count records**. The deduplication pattern the mini project asks for looks like this: ```text 1. HTTP: fetch records from API → many bundles 2. Iterator (if the API returns an array) 3. Data store: Get a record key = {{record_id}} 4. Filter on the line: "Not yet processed" condition: 3.key Does not exist 5. Router → category A route / category B route 6. (in both routes) do the real work 7. Data store: Add/replace a record key = {{record_id}}, processed_at = {{now}} ``` Now re-running the scenario is safe: previously handled IDs get filtered out at step 4. This solves a problem a purely linear, stateless workflow structurally cannot — **there is nowhere else to remember anything**. Without persistence, your only options are re-processing duplicates or relying on the destination system to reject them, which is fragile and often impossible. Beyond data stores, Make also offers **variables** for within-run state: *Set variable* and *Get variable* modules hold a value across modules in the same execution, which is handy for carrying a computed value across a router boundary. ##### Common pitfalls - **Operation explosion.** Iterator over 500 items with six modules after it is 3,000+ operations from one run. Filter before iterating. - **Aggregator with the wrong source module.** Symptom: you still get one output per item, or you aggregate the whole scenario. - **Forgetting the fallback route.** Records matching no filter vanish silently. - **Expecting router branches to share data.** Each route has its own module numbering; you can reference upstream modules, not sibling branches. - **Data store keys that are not unique.** Using an email as a key breaks when two people share one; using a timestamp breaks when two events arrive in the same second. - **Data store size limits.** Storage is capped by plan — prune old records or you will hit a wall mid-run. - **Assuming an array is always an array.** Some APIs return a single object when there is one result and an array when there are many. Guard for it. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task is the core skill: build a scenario with an **Iterator that splits an array** and creates one sheet row per item, then add an **Aggregator** producing a single summary message of all items. Watch the bundle counts on each module — seeing "3 bundles" on the iterator and "1 bundle" on the aggregator is the moment the loop model becomes concrete. The mini project combines all four tools: fetch multiple records from an API, use a **Router** to handle two categories differently, and use a **Data store** so re-runs skip already-processed IDs. Deliberately run it twice and confirm the second run does nothing. That "it correctly did nothing" moment is a real engineering milestone. For the assignment, explain the **Iterator/Aggregator pairing** with a concrete example (the three-item order works well) and name a problem only a data store solves — deduplication across runs is the cleanest answer. ##### Key takeaways - Routers fan a bundle out to every route; per-route filters decide which run, and a fallback route catches everything unmatched. - Filters live on connection lines, cost zero operations, and should be placed as early as possible. - Iterators split one bundle containing an array into many bundles — this is how you stop processing only the first item. - Aggregators (text, array, numeric, table) fold those bundles back into one; the Source Module setting defines the loop boundary. - Data stores give scenarios memory across runs, enabling deduplication, counters and last-sync tracking that stateless workflows cannot do.
